messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur was sixty-eight when he finally sat in the intake room, his hands resting heavily on his knees. The trauma had unfolded years earlier, not with a gradual erosion of trust, but with a sudden, brutal ambush by a romantic partner in the narrow service lane behind his home. His abuser had pursued him on a bicycle, matching his frantic pace until Arthur felt the cold reality of being trapped between a moving frame and a brick wall. The violence that followed shattered his foundational beliefs about how the world works, leaving him convinced that people are not what they seem and that his own judgment was profoundly inadequate. When he later encountered a bicycle passing his office window, found himself alone with a female colleague in a cramped conference room, or navigated the packed aisles of a university hospital, those specific situations would instantly pull him back to the service lane. The environmental cues did not merely remind him of the past; they actively reinforced his catastrophic beliefs, convincing him that the world remained fundamentally hostile and that he was perpetually vulnerable. Over the ensuing months, his clinical environment became both a testing ground and a trap. Working as a psychologist in a bustling city practice, Arthur found that constant threat monitoring had rewired his nervous system. He woke during the night repeatedly, convinced a break-in was imminent, and found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day because the darkness amplifies every shadow. Because he believed the world was shattered and people were untrustworthy, this night-time uncertainty cemented his negative appraisals, while his hypervigilance, in turn, made him interpret neutral stimuli like bicycles and crowded rooms as immediate threats. His conviction that he was inadequate and that others were dangerous actively heightened his sensitivity to these triggers, so a passing bicycle or a sudden crowd instantly registered as danger. To survive the daytime, he enacted strict behavioral controls. He began avoiding wearing similar clothes to his abuser, not out of aesthetic preference, but because the fabric against his skin felt like a trigger waiting to ignite panic. When crowds pressed around him at departmental seminars or when he had to be alone with a woman to discuss a case, his body would stiffen, his eyes would dart across the room looking for harm, and he would never allow himself to feel or express anger. He told himself he was maintaining professional decorum, but the rigid suppression of his emotions only served to isolate the trauma further. His constant checking and night-time alertness prevented proper memory processing, leaving recall stuck in disjointed, photographic frames of that afternoon, or flooded him with raw fear completely divorced from any clear image. By refusing to process the emotional intensity of the event, he ensured his recall remained fragmented. The inability to tell a coherent story of the event only deepened his sense of inadequacy, proving to him that he could not even process the trauma correctly. These fragmented recollections, in turn, solidified his conviction that people are not what they seem, turning every professional interaction into a potential threat. The avoidance of certain garments and the emotion control only heightened his sensitivity to environmental cues, so a sudden bicycle bell or a shift in a crowded hallway would immediately spike his heart rate and pull him back into that initial paralysis. Now, after years of functioning on autopilot while his marriage frayed under the weight of his distance, Arthur had come to believe that his own coping mechanisms were failing him. He sought help not because he wanted to relive the abuse, but because the tighter the cycle grew, the less he could trust his own perception of reality. He hoped to regain a sense of safety that no longer depended on constant vigilance, afraid that another year of suppression would leave him completely isolated from the life and relationships he still valued.
